title: Reading a Leave and Earnings Statement Like an Underwriter: Military Income, the ETS Date and VA Residual Income for an AI Income Agent
summary: A servicemember's Leave and Earnings Statement carries taxable base pay, nontaxable allowances that depend on duty station and dependents, allotments that can reveal debts the credit report does not show, and an expiration of term of service date that decides whether the income continues. A technical account of what our income agent reads from an LES, how it handles a PCS move and an ETS inside twelve months, and how VA's residual income test in 38 CFR 36.4340 is computed and cited.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Heads of underwriting and VA lending at lenders with a military or veteran borrower base, income analysts who see LES documents every week, and QC managers who find the military income defects after closing. Also compliance officers who own SCRA and VA program compliance.


## One Page, Several Kinds of Income


A Leave and Earnings Statement looks like a paystub and is not read like one. On a single month's LES, base pay is taxable. The Basic Allowance for Housing and the Basic Allowance for Subsistence are not taxed, and BAH depends on the duty station's housing area, the member's pay grade and whether they have dependents. Special and incentive pays, such as flight pay or hazardous duty pay, have their own continuance questions. Pay earned in a combat zone may be excluded from income tax under[26 U.S.C. 112](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/26/112) , which changes the taxable figure for the months the member was deployed. And the LES carries an expiration of term of service date, the ETS, which decides whether any of it continues.


An agent that treats the LES as a paystub, adding up the entitlements column and calling it monthly income, gets the gross figure roughly right and gets almost everything else wrong: which parts are taxable, which are stable, which change when the member moves, and whether the service itself continues past the first years of the loan.


## What the Agent Extracts


The[Indexing Agent](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/indexing-agent) classifies the LES as its own document type, distinct from a civilian paystub, because the fields and the rules differ. The[Income Desk](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/income-desk) then extracts each entitlement as its own line with its tax treatment, the deductions and allotments, the leave balance, the pay period, the pay grade and years of service, and the ETS date. Each value is stored in the[Loan Graph](https://www.seiright.com/platform/loan-graph) with the page and position it came from, so the qualifying figure can be traced to the line on the LES that produced it.


The allotments section deserves its own attention. An allotment is a standing deduction the member directs to a third party: a car loan, a personal loan, child support, a savings account, a charity. Some of those are debts that also appear on the credit report. Some do not, because the lender does not report to the bureaus or the obligation is a court order. An underwriter who reads the allotments carefully will sometimes find a monthly obligation missing from the debt-to-income ratio. The agent compares each allotment's payee and amount with the credit report's tradelines and the borrower's declared liabilities, and an allotment it cannot match is a named question for the underwriter rather than something the agent decides is or is not a debt. Our post on[liabilities and DTI reconciliation](https://www.seiright.com/blog/student-loan-liabilities-dti-reconciliation-ai-underwriting-save-rap-fannie-b3-6-05) covers the wider reconciliation this feeds.


## The ETS Inside Twelve Months


Military income is stable for as long as the member keeps serving. When the ETS falls within twelve months of the loan closing, VA's[Lender's Handbook, VA Pamphlet 26-7](https://www.benefits.va.gov/WARMS/pam26_7.asp) , Chapter 4, requires the lender to establish that the income will continue, with evidence such as proof that the member has already reenlisted or extended, a verified offer of civilian employment after separation, or a statement from the member's commanding officer that the member is eligible and expected to reenlist. Agency and investor rules for conventional and FHA loans ask the same continuance question in their own terms.


The agent computes months to ETS from the projected closing date, not today's date, because a file started eleven months before ETS closes inside the window. When the ETS is inside twelve months, it does three things. It asks for the evidence through the[Document Concierge](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/document-concierge) , naming the options the program accepts rather than sending a generic request. It holds the income as unverified for continuance in the Loan Graph, so no condition that depends on it can clear. And when the evidence arrives, it checks it against the rule: a reenlistment contract has a new ETS date, a civilian offer has an employer, a start date and a salary, and a commanding officer's statement has a signature and a date.


What the agent does not do is decide that a career service member with eighteen years in will obviously reenlist. That inference may well be right, and it is still the underwriter's to make, with the evidence or the program's exception process. The agent's job is to make sure the question was asked and answered in the file.


## The PCS Move and the Wrong BAH


Many military borrowers buy because they have orders to a new duty station. The LES in the file shows the BAH for the current station, and the member will be paid the BAH for the new one, which can be hundreds of dollars a month different in either direction. Qualifying on the current BAH overstates or understates the income the borrower will have while paying this mortgage.


So the agent looks for permanent change of station orders in the file and reads the new duty station and report date from them. When the property is near the new station and the orders are present, it flags that the BAH on the LES may not reflect post-move income and states the new station, so the underwriter can apply the BAH rate for the new location and dependency status from the Defense Department's published rates. When the property is far from any duty station on the orders, it raises that as a question too, because it bears on occupancy as well as income.


## VA Residual Income, Computed and Cited


VA underwrites with two tests, and the second is the one civilian underwriting does not have. Under[38 CFR 36.4340](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-38/chapter-I/part-36/subpart-B/section-36.4340) , VA looks at the debt-to-income ratio, with 41% as the benchmark, and at residual income: the money left each month after taxes, the housing payment, other obligations and maintenance and utility costs, compared with a guideline that varies by region, family size and loan amount. When the ratio exceeds 41%, the loan needs a second-level review and a written justification unless residual income exceeds the guideline by at least 20%. VA's guidance also allows the residual income guideline to be reduced by 5% for active duty or retired members who will keep using the benefits of a nearby military installation.


Each piece of that calculation has a judgment buried in it. Taxes are deducted from taxable income only, so getting BAH and BAS treated as nontaxable is the difference between a residual income figure that passes and one that fails. Family size counts everyone in the household who depends on the borrower's income, which is a fact the application captures and the LES dependency status should agree with. The region comes from the property's state. The maintenance and utility estimate comes from the home's square footage and VA's per-square-foot factor. The 5% reduction needs a factual basis that the member will use base facilities.


The Income Desk computes residual income line by line, cites each input to its source and each guideline value to the VA table and region it used, and runs the 20% test when the ratio is above 41%. The result goes through[Triple Check](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#triple-check) before it reaches the LOS: an independent checker recomputes residual income from the extracted values without seeing the maker's figure, and a disagreement stops the work. A file over 41% without the 20% margin is never cleared by the agent. It goes to the underwriter with the calculation and the rule, because the regulation assigns the justification to a person, and the supervisor's sign-off is the control.


## Where Compliance Sits Around the Income


Two other rules touch these files. The Servicemembers Civil Relief Act caps interest at 6% on obligations a member took on before active duty, under[50 U.S.C. 3937](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/3937) . A pre-service debt on the credit report may be showing the capped payment, and the underwriter has to decide what payment to use for the ratio once service ends. The agent flags debts that appear to carry SCRA-reduced payments rather than picking one. Our post on[SCRA compliance](https://www.seiright.com/blog/scra-compliance-ai-agents-servicemembers-dmdc) covers the servicing side.


A member who is deployed may have an active duty alert on their credit file, which changes what the lender must do before extending credit, and which our post on[credit report fraud and active duty alerts](https://www.seiright.com/blog/credit-report-fraud-alert-active-duty-alert-address-discrepancy-mortgage-ai-fcra-605a) covers in detail. The Military Lending Act, by contrast, does not apply: its regulation at 32 CFR 232.3 excludes credit secured by residential real property, which the agent's Rulebook records so the question does not get raised on every VA file.


Ability-to-repay applies to all of it. Under[12 CFR 1026.43(c)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/43/) , the creditor has to verify the income it relies on with reasonably reliable third-party records, and an LES is one, as are the reenlistment contract and the PCS orders when the income depends on them.


## What This Looks Like at QC


Military income defects found after closing are usually one of a few: an ETS inside twelve months with no continuance evidence, BAH from the old duty station, combat pay counted as if it continued after redeployment, or residual income computed with taxes on the allowances. Each one is a question the file could have answered before funding. In the[pre-close QC deployment at Better Mortgage](https://www.seiright.com/case-study/sei-x-nasdaq-lender) , the agent reviews Conventional, FHA, VA and HELOC files across more than twenty document types, and human review per loan file fell from 4 hours 50 minutes to 47 minutes. VA files are where line-level citations matter most, because the residual income worksheet has a dozen inputs and a reviewer needs to see where each one came from.


Sei AI's Income Desk reads the LES as a military document because that is what it is. The underwriting judgment stays where VA and the agencies put it, and the agent's work is to put each judgment in front of the underwriter with the evidence already attached.
